newsitem.title: MACAU: Portuguese president to proceed with China visit.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese president to proceed with China visit.

text.p: Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio, who arrived in Macau on Tuesday, will proceed with his visit to China next week irrespective of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's health, a Chinese official in Macau said on Tuesday. "It will go ahead definitely, irrespective of the state of health of Deng Xiaoping at that time," the official said shortly before Sampaio's arrival in the Portuguese-run enclave on China's southern coast.
China on Tuesday played down fears over the health of Deng that were raised after Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin cut short an out-of-town trip to visit the ailing patriarch.
Sampaio, making his first visit to Macau since his election to president in January, said in Lisbon last week he would discuss the enclave's transition to Chinese rule on December 20th, 1999.
He said he had "no illusions that what will happen in Hong Kong will influence Macau". The British colony of Hong Kong reverts to China on July 1 this year.
Lisbon expects Beijing to continue to recognise the ban on capital punishment in Macau when the territory reverted to China, Sampaio said.
China executed several thousand people last year in a nationwide crackdown on crime.

The President said Portugual and China had reached an understanding on capital punishment. "I take it for granted (that the death penalty ban will be respected by China beyond 1999), because there were, obviously, consultations on the matter," Sampaio said.
Macau, on China's southern coast some 60 km (40 miles) across the Pearl River delta from Hong Kong, was settled by Portugal in 1557.
Beijing has promised both territories considerable autonomy in running their affairs and to permit them to retain their capitalist way of life after they return to China's fold.
Chinese officials posted to Macau have indicated that the death ban will be respected by Beijing since it was part of Macau's judicial heritage.
Sampaio said in an arrival statement he was confident that Macau's identity and way of life would be preserved beyond the handover.
Sampaio said Lisbon and Beijing were still negotiating the nationality rights of Macau's 10,000-strong Eurasian minority, the Macanese.
Most hold Portuguese passports and want to hang on to them after 1999 while retaining their status as Macau residents.
Portugal recognises dual nationality but China does not.
About 110,000 of Macau's 455,000 residents are Portuguese passport holders. Most of the others are immigrants from China.

Sampaio is scheduled to meet President Jiang Zemin, Premier Li Peng, and Qiao Shi, chairman of the standing committee of the National People's Congress, or parliament, during his visit to China from Sunday.
